title: Java Mastery: From Fundamentals to JVM and Production Engineering
subtitle: A comprehensive path from Java syntax and object-oriented programming to collections, concurrency, JVM internals, performance, security, architecture, and senior-level interview preparation.

chapters.title: Java Foundations
chapters.summary: Understand Java's history, platform model, source-to-bytecode pipeline, JDK/JRE/JVM roles, program structure, and the modern development workflow.

sections.title: What Is Java?

callout.title: Mental model
callout.message: Think of Java as a language plus a runtime ecosystem. The JVM is the execution engine; the JDK is the developer toolkit.

keyTakeaways: Java source is normally compiled to JVM bytecode.
Portability comes from the JVM abstraction and standardized runtime behavior.
The language, JVM, and JDK are related but are not the same thing.

sections.title: JDK, JRE, and JVM
sections.content:
The **JVM** executes Java bytecode and provides runtime services such as class loading, memory management, garbage collection, synchronization, and JIT compilation. The **JDK** is the developer distribution: it includes the runtime plus tools such as `javac`, `java`, `jar`, and diagnostic utilities.

The term **JRE** historically referred to a runtime distribution containing the JVM and runtime libraries. Modern JDK distributions generally provide the complete runtime image themselves, so treating "install a separate JRE" as the normal development workflow is outdated.

A useful hierarchy is:

`JDK = development tools + runtime`

`JVM = engine that executes JVM bytecode`

```text
Java source (.java)
     |
     | javac
     v
Bytecode (.class)
     |
     | JVM class loader + verifier
     v
JVM execution engine
     |
     +--> Interpreter
     +--> JIT compiler
     +--> Garbage collector
     +--> Runtime libraries
```

callout.title: Interview shortcut
callout.message: Java source is compiled to bytecode, then the JVM can interpret and JIT-compile that bytecode at runtime.

keyTakeaways: `javac` compiles Java source into bytecode.
The JVM executes bytecode and may compile hot code to native instructions.
Modern Java development normally starts with a JDK.

sections.title: Program Structure and the Entry Point
keyTakeaways: Java is case-sensitive.
The `main` method is a static entry point for conventional command-line applications.
Packages provide namespace organization and support access control.

sections.title: Compile, Run, Package, and Inspect
sections.content:
A minimal workflow is: write source, compile it, run it, package it when needed, and inspect artifacts or diagnostics when something fails.

```bash
javac Application.java
java Application
jar --create --file app.jar --main-class Application Application.class
java -jar app.jar
```

For real projects, Maven or Gradle normally handles dependency resolution, compilation, testing, packaging, code quality, and publishing. The command-line tools remain important because they reveal what the build tool is doing underneath.

Compilation errors are caught before execution. Runtime failures such as `NullPointerException`, `ClassNotFoundException`, or an out-of-memory condition happen after compilation and require different debugging techniques.

callout.title: Build-tool principle
callout.message: Learn the JDK commands even if you use Maven or Gradle; they make build failures easier to reason about.

keyTakeaways: `javac` compiles source; `java` launches a class; `jar` packages artifacts.
Build tools automate repetitive workflows but do not replace understanding the JDK tools.
Compilation success does not guarantee runtime correctness.

chapters.title: Types, Variables, Operators, and Control Flow
chapters.summary: Master Java primitive and reference types, conversions, operators, expressions, branching, loops, arrays, and command-line data.

sections.title: Primitive Types vs Reference Types
keyTakeaways: Primitive and reference types have different semantics.
`String` and arrays are reference types.
Choose numeric types based on range and precision requirements.

sections.title: Conversions, Casting, Autoboxing, and Unboxing

callout.title: Beware unboxing
callout.message: A nullable `Integer` is not interchangeable with an `int`; unboxing `null` throws `NullPointerException`.

keyTakeaways: Widening conversions generally preserve the value.
Narrowing casts may truncate or overflow.
Autoboxing is convenient but does not remove allocation and nullability concerns.

sections.title: Operators and Expressions
keyTakeaways: `&&` and `||` short-circuit.
`==` is not a general replacement for `.equals()`.
Use parentheses to make non-obvious precedence explicit.

sections.title: Branching and Loops
keyTakeaways: Use switch expressions when a branch naturally produces a value.
Enhanced `for` improves readability for collection traversal.
Choose loops and streams based on clarity and semantics.

chapters.title: Object-Oriented Programming
chapters.summary: Build robust Java models using classes, constructors, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces, composition, records, and sealed types.

sections.title: Classes, Objects, Fields, and Constructors
keyTakeaways: Constructors should establish invariants.
Encapsulation keeps object state under controlled mutation.
Prefer immutable fields when the domain allows it.

sections.title: Encapsulation, Inheritance, and Polymorphism

callout.title: Prefer composition
callout.message: Inheritance creates tight coupling. Use composition when the relationship is really 'has-a' rather than 'is-a'.

keyTakeaways: Polymorphism reduces coupling to concrete implementations.
Interfaces are excellent boundaries for dependency injection and testing.
Composition is often more flexible than deep inheritance hierarchies.

sections.title: Abstract Classes and Interfaces
keyTakeaways: A class has single inheritance but can implement multiple interfaces.
Abstract classes are useful when shared state or implementation is intrinsic.
Interfaces define capabilities and reduce dependency on concrete classes.

sections.title: Records, Sealed Classes, and Enums
keyTakeaways: Records reduce boilerplate for data-centric types.
Sealed types make an inheritance boundary explicit.
Records are shallowly immutable; referenced mutable objects can still change.

chapters.title: Methods, Arrays, Strings, and Object Contracts
chapters.summary: Learn method design, varargs, recursion, arrays, String behavior, immutability, equals/hashCode, toString, and object-level contracts.

sections.title: Methods, Parameters, Return Values, and Varargs

callout.title: Pass-by-value
callout.message: Java never passes variables by reference. A reference value can be copied, and both variables can point to the same object.

keyTakeaways: Java is strictly pass-by-value.
Varargs provide convenient variable-length arguments.
Method contracts should make inputs, outputs, and failure behavior explicit.

sections.title: Arrays and Multidimensional Data
keyTakeaways: Arrays have fixed length.
Array indexing starts at zero.
A Java `T[][]` is an array whose elements are themselves arrays.

sections.title: String Immutability and StringBuilder

callout.title: String equality
callout.message: Use `equals()` for string content. `==` compares reference identity for objects.

keyTakeaways: Strings are immutable.
Use `StringBuilder` for repeated string construction.
String pooling is not a reason to use `==` for value comparison.

sections.title: equals, hashCode, and toString Contracts
sections.content:
`equals()` defines logical equality when overridden. `hashCode()` must be consistent with `equals`: equal objects must have equal hash codes. `toString()` provides a readable representation for logs and debugging.

```java
public record UserKey(String tenantId, String userId) {}
```

For mutable classes used as `HashMap` keys, changing fields involved in equality after insertion can make the entry effectively unreachable.

The equality relation should be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and false for comparison with `null`.
keyTakeaways: `equals` defines logical equality.
Equal objects must have equal hash codes.
Do not mutate equality-defining state of a key while it is stored in a hash-based collection.

chapters.title: Collections and Generics
chapters.summary: Master List, Set, Map, Queue, Deque, iterators, sorting, generics, wildcards, type erasure, and collection selection.

sections.title: List, Set, and Map
keyTakeaways: Choose collections based on required semantics.
`ArrayList` is a strong default for indexed/sequential lists.
Hash-based structures depend on correct `equals` and `hashCode`.

sections.title: Queues, Deques, and Priority Queues
keyTakeaways: `ArrayDeque` can serve as both stack and queue.
`PriorityQueue` exposes priority order through removal/peek, not full iteration order.
Use queue APIs such as `offer` and `poll` for clear semantics.

sections.title: Generics and Wildcards

callout.title: PECS
callout.message: Use `extends` when you mainly read values as a base type; use `super` when you mainly write values of a subtype.

keyTakeaways: Generics catch many type errors at compile time.
`? extends T` is producer-oriented; `? super T` is consumer-oriented.
Java generics use type erasure rather than fully reified generic types.

sections.title: Sorting, Comparators, and Iterators
keyTakeaways: Use `Comparable` for natural order and `Comparator` for alternate orders.
Comparator contracts must be consistent.
Use collection APIs instead of reimplementing common traversal logic.

chapters.title: Exceptions and Error Handling
chapters.summary: Understand checked and unchecked exceptions, try/catch/finally, try-with-resources, custom exceptions, propagation, and resilient error handling.

sections.title: Exception Hierarchy and Checked vs Unchecked
keyTakeaways: Checked exceptions are enforced by the compiler.
Unchecked exceptions include many invalid-state and programming failures.
Preserve the original cause when wrapping exceptions.

sections.title: try, catch, finally, and Exception Propagation

callout.title: Avoid empty catches
callout.message: An empty catch block silently discards failures and makes production diagnosis extremely difficult.

keyTakeaways: Catch exceptions where you can make a meaningful decision.
Preserve context and causes when rethrowing.
Do not use exceptions as normal high-frequency control flow.

sections.title: Try-with-Resources
keyTakeaways: Prefer try-with-resources for `AutoCloseable` resources.
Resources close in reverse declaration order.
Suppressed exceptions preserve cleanup failures without losing the original exception.

sections.title: Custom Exceptions and Error Strategy
keyTakeaways: Exceptions are part of an API's behavioral contract.
Wrap low-level failures when a higher-level abstraction has more meaning.
Keep sensitive information out of exception messages and logs.

chapters.title: JVM, Class Loading, and Runtime Memory
chapters.summary: Go beneath the language into class loading, bytecode, runtime data areas, stack frames, heap, metaspace, JIT compilation, and JVM diagnostics.

sections.title: Class Loading, Linking, and Initialization
sections.content:
Before a class can be used, the JVM loads its class representation, verifies and prepares it, resolves symbolic references as required, and initializes static state when initialization is triggered.

Class loaders form a delegation hierarchy. Loader identity is part of a class's runtime identity, so the same binary name loaded by different defining loaders represents distinct runtime types.

```java
Class<?> type = Class.forName("java.lang.String");
System.out.println(type.getClassLoader());
```

This enables plugins and isolation while also creating class-loader leak risks when long-lived references retain unloadable class loaders.
keyTakeaways: Loading, linking, and initialization are distinct concepts.
Class identity includes the defining class loader.
Custom class loaders are powerful but add lifecycle complexity.

sections.title: JVM Runtime Data Areas

diagram.title: Simplified JVM Runtime Areas
diagram.code:
flowchart TD
A[Java Application] --> B[Class Loader]
B --> C[Runtime Data Areas]
C --> D[Heap]
C --> E[Thread Stacks]
C --> F[Class Metadata]
C --> G[PC Register]
C --> H[Native Method Stack]
C --> I[Execution Engine]

keyTakeaways: The heap is shared; each thread has its own JVM stack.
Stack frames represent active method invocations.
JVM specification concepts and HotSpot implementation details should not be conflated.

sections.title: Interpreter, JIT, and Hot Code
sections.content:
The JVM can interpret bytecode and compile frequently executed code to native machine instructions using JIT compilation. Runtime profiling allows optimizations such as inlining, dead-code elimination, escape analysis, and speculative optimization.

```text
Bytecode
   |
   +--> Interpreter --> execution
   |
   +--> JIT compiler --> native code --> optimized hot path
                              |
                              +--> deoptimization if assumptions fail
```

This means startup and steady-state performance can differ. Benchmarking Java requires warm-up, realistic workloads, and proper measurement.

callout.title: Benchmarking
callout.message: Do not conclude that one Java implementation is faster from a tiny cold-start benchmark; JIT warm-up matters.

keyTakeaways: JIT compilation is profile-guided and runtime-aware.
Optimized code can be deoptimized when assumptions fail.
Use proper benchmarking methodology.

sections.title: JVM Diagnostics and Troubleshooting
sections.content:
Production debugging should start with evidence. Useful tools include `jcmd`, `jstack`, `jmap`, Java Flight Recorder, Java Mission Control, and JVM logging facilities.

```bash
jcmd <pid> VM.flags
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info
jcmd <pid> Thread.print
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=recording.jfr
```

Thread dumps help identify deadlocks and blocked threads. Heap information helps investigate memory pressure. Flight Recorder captures runtime events for CPU, allocation, locks, I/O, and GC analysis.

The workflow is: observe, collect evidence, form a hypothesis, make a targeted change, and verify.
keyTakeaways: Use thread dumps for thread-state problems.
Use heap/GC evidence for memory problems.
Java Flight Recorder is valuable for correlating CPU, allocation, locks, and GC behavior.

chapters.title: Lambdas, Functional Interfaces, Streams, and Optional
chapters.summary: Use Java's functional programming features effectively with lambdas, method references, streams, collectors, parallel streams, and Optional.

sections.title: Lambdas and Functional Interfaces
keyTakeaways: A lambda targets a functional interface.
Method references can improve readability.
Prefer small, intention-revealing lambdas.

sections.title: Stream Pipelines
sections.content:
Streams provide a declarative way to process sequences. A pipeline typically has a source, intermediate operations, and a terminal operation.

```java
List<String> names = List.of("Java", "Kotlin", "JavaScript");

List<String> result = names.stream()
    .filter(name -> name.startsWith("J"))
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .toList();
```

Intermediate operations such as `filter`, `map`, `sorted`, and `distinct` are generally lazy. A terminal operation such as `toList`, `count`, `findFirst`, or `forEach` drives execution.

Streams are not collections and are usually single-use.

callout.title: Lazy evaluation
callout.message: Calling `filter()` or `map()` alone does not process elements. A terminal operation drives the pipeline.

keyTakeaways: Streams are pipelines, not storage containers.
Intermediate operations are generally lazy.
A stream should normally be consumed once.

sections.title: Collectors, Grouping, and Reduction
sections.content:
Collectors turn streams into lists, sets, maps, grouped structures, and summaries.

```java
Map<Integer, List<String>> byLength =
    names.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length));

int totalLength =
    names.stream()
        .mapToInt(String::length)
        .sum();
```

`groupingBy` is useful for classification. `partitioningBy` splits values into two groups. Reduction operations combine elements into a result.

Prefer built-in collectors when they express the operation clearly. Custom collectors require careful supplier, accumulator, combiner, and finisher design.
keyTakeaways: Use `groupingBy` for classification and aggregation.
Primitive streams can reduce boxing for numeric operations.
Custom collectors must account for sequential and parallel semantics.

sections.title: Optional and Absence Modeling
sections.content:
`Optional<T>` models a value that may be absent. It is most useful as a return type when absence is a meaningful outcome.

```java
Optional<String> username = findUsername();

String display = username
    .map(String::trim)
    .filter(value -> !value.isEmpty())
    .orElse("anonymous");
```

Avoid using `Optional` as a field or parameter by default. `orElse` evaluates its fallback immediately, while `orElseGet` evaluates a supplier lazily.

Avoid `get()` without first establishing presence.

callout.title: Optional is not a magic null killer
callout.message: Use Optional deliberately at API boundaries where absence is part of the contract.

keyTakeaways: Use Optional to model meaningful absence.
`orElseGet` is lazy; `orElse` evaluates its argument eagerly.
Avoid unsafe `Optional.get()` patterns.

chapters.title: Date-Time, I/O, NIO, and Serialization
chapters.summary: Work correctly with time zones, files, paths, channels, buffers, streams, serialization concepts, and data boundaries.

sections.title: The java.time API

callout.title: Time zones are business data
callout.message: A timestamp without its intended time-zone semantics can be ambiguous.

keyTakeaways: Use `java.time` for new code.
Use `Instant` for absolute points in time.
Use explicit zones for human/business-local schedules.

sections.title: Files, Paths, and I/O Streams
keyTakeaways: `Path` and `Files` are modern NIO.2 APIs.
Choose byte vs character APIs based on data semantics.
Avoid loading huge files into memory when streaming is sufficient.

sections.title: Channels, Buffers, and Non-Blocking I/O
keyTakeaways: Channels transfer data through buffers.
`flip()` prepares a written buffer for reading.
Use NIO directly when its control is valuable; otherwise prefer higher-level abstractions.

sections.title: Serialization and Data Boundaries
sections.content:
Java's built-in object serialization has compatibility and security concerns. For network APIs, JSON, Protobuf, Avro, or other explicit formats are often better because the wire contract is visible and language interoperability is easier.

```java
public record UserDto(String id, String name) {}
```

DTOs separate external representations from internal domain models. If a system consumes untrusted serialized data, treat deserialization as a security boundary and avoid arbitrary object construction.

callout.title: Untrusted deserialization
callout.message: Never treat untrusted serialized object data as harmless input. Prefer explicit, constrained data formats.

keyTakeaways: Wire formats are API contracts.
DTOs protect internal models from external coupling.
Security must be considered at every deserialization boundary.

chapters.title: Concurrency and Multithreading
chapters.summary: Understand threads, executors, synchronization, locks, atomics, visibility, happens-before, concurrent collections, futures, and virtual threads.

sections.title: Threads and Runnable Tasks

callout.title: start vs run
callout.message: `start()` schedules a new thread. `run()` is just an ordinary method call when invoked directly.

keyTakeaways: Prefer task-based concurrency over many manually managed threads.
Thread safety is primarily about shared mutable state.
Know the difference between starting a thread and invoking run directly.

sections.title: synchronized, Locks, and Visibility
keyTakeaways: `synchronized` provides mutual exclusion and visibility.
`volatile` does not make compound read-modify-write operations atomic.
The Java Memory Model defines visibility guarantees.

sections.title: Executors and CompletableFuture
keyTakeaways: Executors control concurrency resources.
`CompletableFuture` enables composition of asynchronous operations.
Thread-pool sizing depends on workload characteristics.

sections.title: Concurrent Collections and Atomics
sections.content:
Java provides `ConcurrentHashMap`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, `BlockingQueue`, and atomic classes such as `AtomicInteger` and `AtomicReference`.

```java
ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> counters =
    new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

counters.computeIfAbsent("java", key -> new LongAdder())
        .increment();
```

Concurrent collections provide well-defined concurrent operations. `LongAdder` can outperform `AtomicLong` under heavy contention because updates are distributed across cells.
keyTakeaways: Use concurrent collections rather than manually synchronizing ordinary collections when appropriate.
Atomics support thread-safe single-variable state transitions.
Contention characteristics should guide counter selection.

sections.title: Virtual Threads and Modern Concurrency

callout.title: Virtual-thread rule
callout.message: Use virtual threads to scale blocking task concurrency, not as a replacement for CPU parallelism or as permission to remove backpressure.

keyTakeaways: Virtual threads are lightweight and suited to many blocking tasks.
They do not increase CPU capacity.
Concurrency still needs limits around external resources.

chapters.title: Memory, Garbage Collection, and Performance
chapters.summary: Understand object allocation, garbage collection, reachability, G1 and other collectors, leaks, allocation pressure, profiling, and performance engineering.

sections.title: Object Lifecycle and Reachability
sections.content:
Java automatically manages object memory. An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when it is no longer reachable from live roots.

```java
Object object = new Object();
object = null;
```

Setting a variable to `null` does not force collection. Static fields, thread locals, caches, listeners, and long-lived collections can accidentally retain objects.

A memory leak in a garbage-collected language is usually a logical retention problem rather than failure to manually free memory.
keyTakeaways: GC eligibility is based on reachability.
A garbage-collected application can still leak memory through unintended retention.
Calling GC explicitly is rarely an appropriate leak fix.

sections.title: Generational Garbage Collection
sections.content:
Many workloads create short-lived objects. Generational strategies exploit this by treating young and older objects differently.

```text
Allocation
   |
   v
Young regions
   |
   | survivors
   v
Older regions
   |
   v
Reclamation / compaction as required
```

Exact mechanics depend on the collector. Modern collectors such as G1 use regions rather than a simple contiguous physical young/old layout.

The performance question is whether allocation rate, live-set size, collector behavior, and pause characteristics match the application's goals.
keyTakeaways: Generational GC exploits object lifetime patterns.
GC performance depends on allocation rate and live-set characteristics.
Measure real allocation and pause behavior before tuning.

sections.title: Modern Collectors: G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah
sections.content:
G1 is a region-based collector designed to balance throughput and pause-time goals. ZGC and Shenandoah emphasize very low pause times through highly concurrent collection techniques.

The correct collector depends on workload, heap size, latency objectives, JVM version, and operational constraints.

```bash
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms2g -Xmx2g -jar app.jar
```

For modern JVMs, use the defaults and tuning guidance for the specific JDK release before adding many flags.

callout.title: Avoid cargo-cult JVM flags
callout.message: GC flags are version- and workload-sensitive. Measure first and consult documentation for the exact JDK release.

keyTakeaways: G1 is a common general-purpose collector.
ZGC and Shenandoah target very low pause behavior.
Collector tuning must be based on the actual JDK version and workload.

sections.title: Memory Leaks and Profiling
keyTakeaways: Look at retained size and reference paths, not only object counts.
Heap dumps answer retention questions; allocation profiling answers creation-rate questions.
Caches need lifecycle or eviction policies.

chapters.title: Modern Java Language Features
chapters.summary: Explore switch expressions, pattern matching, records, sealed classes, text blocks, modules, and modern Java evolution.

sections.title: Switch Expressions
keyTakeaways: Switch expressions return values.
Arrow cases do not fall through by default.
Exhaustiveness can improve safety for closed domains.

sections.title: Pattern Matching
keyTakeaways: Pattern variables eliminate many explicit casts.
Pattern matching works well with sealed hierarchies.
Use it to clarify domain logic.

sections.title: Records and Sealed Hierarchies
keyTakeaways: Records reduce boilerplate for data carriers.
Sealed types explicitly close an inheritance hierarchy.
The combination is useful for finite domain variants.

sections.title: Text Blocks, Modules, and API Evolution
sections.content:
Text blocks improve multiline string readability.

```java
String json = \"\"\"
    {
      "name": "Java",
      "version": 26
    }
    \"\"\";
```

The Java Platform Module System introduced modules, explicit dependencies, and stronger encapsulation. Modules can be valuable for large modular applications, although many server applications still primarily use packages and build-tool dependency management.

When adopting new features, consider the deployed JDK, build plugins, runtime environment, and library compatibility.
keyTakeaways: Text blocks improve multiline string readability.
Modules provide dependency and encapsulation boundaries.
Feature adoption must consider the complete toolchain.

chapters.title: Reflection, Annotations, Modules, and Metaprogramming
chapters.summary: Understand reflection, annotations, dynamic proxies, modules, service loading, and the trade-offs of runtime metaprogramming.

sections.title: Reflection

callout.title: Reflection is a tool, not a design default
callout.message: Prefer normal Java calls for business logic; use reflection when the framework truly needs dynamic discovery.

keyTakeaways: Reflection provides runtime type inspection and invocation.
It trades some compile-time safety for flexibility.
Framework infrastructure is a better home for reflection.

sections.title: Annotations and Metadata
keyTakeaways: Annotations are metadata, not executable behavior by themselves.
Retention determines how long annotation information is available.
Compile-time processing can move work out of runtime.

sections.title: Dynamic Proxies and Service Loading
keyTakeaways: Dynamic proxies are primarily interface-oriented.
Service loading supports pluggable implementations.
Runtime indirection should be documented.

sections.title: JPMS Modules and Strong Encapsulation
keyTakeaways: Packages and modules solve different levels of organization.
`exports` controls cross-module accessibility.
`opens` is relevant to reflective access.

chapters.title: Testing, Maven, Gradle, and Code Quality
chapters.summary: Build production-grade Java projects with Maven or Gradle, unit and integration tests, mocking, dependency management, and quality gates.

sections.title: Maven and Gradle
sections.content:
Maven uses convention, lifecycle phases, and XML project metadata. Gradle uses a programmable build model and supports Groovy or Kotlin DSLs.

```bash
mvn test
mvn package

./gradlew test
./gradlew build
```

A build should be reproducible: dependency versions should be controlled, generated artifacts should be deterministic where practical, and CI should run the same essential verification steps developers use locally.
keyTakeaways: Build tools automate compilation, testing, packaging, and dependency resolution.
Manage dependency versions intentionally.
CI should execute reproducible verification steps.

sections.title: Unit vs Integration Testing
keyTakeaways: Unit tests focus on isolated behavior.
Integration tests validate component interaction.
Fast feedback and realistic coverage are complementary.

sections.title: Mocks, Stubs, Fakes, and Test Doubles
keyTakeaways: Test behavior rather than implementation details.
Fakes can be simpler than large mock configurations.
Mock external boundaries deliberately.

sections.title: Quality Gates and Secure Dependencies
sections.content:
Production Java projects commonly combine formatting, static analysis, tests, dependency scanning, and code review.

Useful checks include compiler warnings, static analyzers, formatting tools, dependency vulnerability scanning, and CI tests.

```bash
mvn test
mvn verify
```

Quality gates should fail the build for issues that matter. Avoid hundreds of noisy warnings that developers learn to ignore.
keyTakeaways: Automate repeatable quality checks.
Dependency security is part of application security.
High-signal quality gates are more effective than noisy rule sets.

chapters.title: Java Backend Engineering
chapters.summary: Connect Java applications to HTTP services and databases, understand JDBC, transactions, connection pools, REST API design, and backend resilience.

sections.title: HTTP Client and REST Fundamentals
sections.content:
Modern Java includes an HTTP client API for synchronous and asynchronous HTTP calls.

```java
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://example.com/api/users"))
    .GET()
    .build();

HttpResponse<String> response =
    client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
```

A production HTTP client needs timeouts, connection reuse, retries where safe, observability, response validation, and protection against unbounded concurrency.
keyTakeaways: HTTP clients need timeouts and resilience policies.
Retries are only safe when operation and server semantics allow them.
API contracts should make validation and error behavior explicit.

sections.title: JDBC and Connection Pools

callout.title: SQL injection
callout.message: Never concatenate untrusted input into SQL. Use prepared statements or a safe data-access abstraction.

keyTakeaways: Use prepared statements for values.
Connection pools are shared scarce resources.
Database pool sizing must account for database capacity.

sections.title: Transactions and Isolation
keyTakeaways: Transactions define atomicity boundaries.
Isolation is a concurrency trade-off.
Keep transaction boundaries aligned with business operations.

sections.title: Timeouts, Retries, Bulkheads, and Backpressure
sections.content:
A service is only as reliable as its dependencies allow. A slow database or API can consume all request resources if there are no timeouts or concurrency limits.

Resilience techniques include deadlines, bounded retries with jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limits, queues, and backpressure.

```text
Request
  |
  v
Timeout --> Retry policy --> Downstream
  |              |
  |              +--> bounded attempts
  v
Fallback / error
```

Observability should include latency, error rate, saturation, dependency timings, and retry counts.
keyTakeaways: Timeouts are mandatory for remote dependencies.
Retries can amplify outages if uncontrolled.
Backpressure and concurrency limits protect downstream systems.

chapters.title: Design Patterns and Java Architecture
chapters.summary: Apply SOLID, common design patterns, dependency inversion, layered architecture, hexagonal architecture, and domain-oriented design.

sections.title: SOLID Principles
keyTakeaways: SOLID is about managing change and coupling.
Dependency inversion improves testability and architectural boundaries.
Do not introduce abstractions without a meaningful reason.

sections.title: Common Patterns in Java
keyTakeaways: Patterns are reusable design ideas, not mandatory class structures.
Strategy uses polymorphism to vary behavior.
Prefer the simplest design that remains easy to change.

sections.title: Layered and Hexagonal Architecture
sections.content:
Layered architecture commonly separates controllers, services, and repositories. Hexagonal architecture separates application/domain logic from external adapters through ports.

```text
HTTP / Messaging / CLI
         |
      Adapters
         |
        Ports
         |
Application / Domain
         |
        Ports
         |
     DB / APIs / Files
```

The key idea is dependency direction: business rules should not be tightly coupled to HTTP frameworks, database drivers, or cloud SDKs.
keyTakeaways: Architecture is primarily about dependency direction.
Ports isolate business logic from infrastructure.
Adapters are translation boundaries, not business-rule containers.

sections.title: Domain Modeling and Maintainability
keyTakeaways: Put important invariants near the model that owns them.
Value objects capture concepts and their rules.
Architecture should reflect real business complexity rather than ceremony.

chapters.title: Java Application Security
chapters.summary: Learn secure input handling, authentication and authorization concepts, cryptography basics, secrets, deserialization risks, and secure dependency practices.

sections.title: Input Validation and Output Encoding
keyTakeaways: Validate at trust boundaries.
Use context-specific encoding and safe APIs.
Validation for one sink does not automatically protect another sink.

sections.title: Authentication vs Authorization
sections.content:
Authentication answers "Who are you?" Authorization answers "What are you allowed to do?"

A secure backend enforces authorization on the server for every protected operation. Hiding UI controls is not authorization.

```text
Request
  |
  v
Authenticate identity
  |
  v
Authorize action/resource
  |
  v
Business operation
```

Sessions, tokens, OAuth/OIDC, and API keys solve different problems. Choose based on system boundaries.
keyTakeaways: Authentication and authorization are different concerns.
Authorization must be enforced server-side.
Use established protocols instead of custom authentication schemes.

sections.title: Cryptography and Secret Management

callout.title: Never commit secrets
callout.message: Treat leaked credentials as compromised; rotate them and use secret management.

keyTakeaways: Do not implement cryptographic primitives yourself.
Use dedicated password hashing for passwords.
Keep secrets out of source code and ordinary logs.

sections.title: Deserialization and Dependency Security
sections.content:
Java applications depend heavily on third-party libraries. A vulnerability in a transitive dependency can become a production risk.

Use dependency scanning, timely patching, software bills of materials where appropriate, and minimal dependency sets. For deserialization, prefer explicit schemas and constrained types over arbitrary object graphs from untrusted input.

```bash
mvn dependency:tree
./gradlew dependencies
```

Security is a lifecycle concern: secure coding, dependency management, CI scanning, runtime hardening, logging, incident response, and patching all matter.
keyTakeaways: Transitive dependencies are part of your attack surface.
Prefer explicit data formats for untrusted input.
Security needs continuous maintenance.

chapters.title: Production Java: Packaging, Deployment, and Observability
chapters.summary: Prepare Java services for production with executable JARs, containers, configuration, logging, metrics, tracing, health checks, and operational readiness.

sections.title: Packaging and Containers
sections.content:
Java applications can be packaged as JARs and deployed directly or inside containers.

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY app.jar /app/app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]
```

The runtime image should match the supported JDK/runtime and patch strategy. Avoid embedding secrets in image layers.
keyTakeaways: Build artifacts should be immutable and reproducible.
Runtime configuration belongs outside the image.
Use a supported, patched Java runtime image.

sections.title: Configuration and Environment Management
keyTakeaways: Validate configuration at startup.
Keep secrets separate from ordinary configuration.
Never log sensitive configuration values.

sections.title: Logging, Metrics, and Distributed Tracing
sections.content:
Logs explain events; metrics explain trends; traces explain request flow across services.

```java
logger.info("Order completed: orderId={}, durationMs={}",
            orderId, durationMs);
```

Useful production metrics include request rate, error rate, latency, saturation, queue depth, database pool usage, and JVM/GC health. Observability data itself should be treated as sensitive.
keyTakeaways: Use logs, metrics, and traces together.
Correlation IDs make distributed debugging easier.
Observability data must be treated as sensitive production data.

sections.title: Health Checks and Graceful Shutdown
sections.content:
Production services need readiness and liveness concepts. Readiness answers whether the service should receive traffic; liveness answers whether the process is alive enough for the platform to keep it running.

Graceful shutdown stops accepting new work, allows in-flight work to finish within a deadline, closes resources, and exits.

```text
SIGTERM
  |
  v
Stop new traffic
  |
  v
Finish in-flight work
  |
  v
Close pools / clients
  |
  v
Exit
```
keyTakeaways: Readiness and liveness serve different purposes.
Graceful shutdown prevents dropped work during deployments.
Health checks should reflect meaningful service capability.
